title: Time‐Intensity Trade‐Off of Water‐Use Efficiency in Piper nigrum
content: Water-use efficiency (WUE) is a crucial parameter for sustainable crop production, particularly in water-limited environments where optimizing resource utilization is essential for maintaining productivity and resilience. This study investigates the physiological and agronomic responses of two black pepper (Piper nigrum) cultivars, Clonada and Uthirankotta, under varying soil water potentials and along the time. Results indicate that WUE varies significantly between cultivars due to distinct physiological strategies. Clonada exhibited higher photosynthetic rates, stomatal conductance, and gas exchange efficiency, leading to greater yield performance under moderate stress conditions. Conversely, Uthirankotta demonstrated consistently higher WUE across all water conditions, prioritizing water conservation and biomass accumulation over gas exchange efficiency. Both cultivars displayed peak performance at 25–35 kPa soil water potential, with yield and physiological efficiency declining at higher tensions. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) confirmed distinct physiological profiles, reinforcing the trade-offs between productivity and water-use strategies. These findings highlight the importance of cultivar selection for optimizing WUE in black pepper cultivation and provide insights for improving irrigation management and breeding programs.
